Odious

/OH-dee-uhs/ - the stress falls on OH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Odious means instilling hatred or intense displeasure.

The bridge company doubled the toll again at harvest, making itself odious to every farmer in the valley.

Worked Example

The clause was buried on page nine: tenants who fell behind would owe, on top of everything else, the cost of their own eviction paperwork. Even the other landlords at the association meeting went quiet when it was read aloud. By spring, 'the paperwork clause' had become shorthand across the county for everything hateful about the housing market.

Odious is the exact word because it describes the thing that makes people hate it — the quality lives in the object. A clause, a tax, a practice, a villain: whatever earns loathing at first description is odious. Note the direction: malicious (this unit's cousin) judges the doer's intent; odious judges how the deed strikes everyone else.

How Odious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

hateful

hateful: the plain twin — stirring up the same hatred

loathsome

loathsome: adds a shudder of disgust to the hatred

Antonyms

delightful

delightful: stirring pleasure instead

endearing

endearing: winning affection at first meeting

How Strong Is It? — disagreeable → odious → abominable

disagreeable vs. odious

disagreeable vs. odious: Disagreeable earns a frown and a complaint; odious earns real hatred.

abominable vs. odious

abominable vs. odious: Abominable goes past odious — the thing is beyond bearing, fit only to be stamped out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — odi

Root — odi: hatred (Latin odium)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Odi- (hatred — Latin odium) + -ous (full of) = full of hatred — not the hatred it feels, but the hatred it draws. Latin odium was the loathing itself; an odious thing is soaked in it, collecting hatred the way a lit window collects looks.

Use the root in a new word: annoy

Use the root in a new word: annoy: To annoy comes from Latin in odio — literally to make yourself hateful to someone, one small irritation at a time.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Odious is strong: not merely unpleasant but hatred-earning, and a touch bookish — laws, clauses, villains, practices. For a person's harmful intent, this unit's malicious is the word; odious describes how the result strikes the rest of us. If the offense is only mildly off-putting, say that instead — calling a squeaky chair odious spends the word where it isn't owed.
